markdown:
# What can you do when the holiday rush fills your mind? A one-verse pause with Daily Dhamma

That is the exact opening line of our App Store listing today: "Holiday rush filling your mind? One Buddha verse from the Dhammapada a day and a gentle 'Are you present right now?' reminder to return to calm. Save verses that stay."

We wrote that line because the end of November is when our own minds feel most crowded — messages to answer, travel to plan, work to close, and a low background hum that there is still something we forgot. We built Daily Dhamma, listed on the App Store as Dhamma Quotes: Buddha Quotes, as a response that stays deliberately small. This guide explains, in our own words as the makers, how we use that one-verse pause during a busy season, what the app actually does and does not do, and what our measured App Store numbers say so far.

## Why does the holiday rush feel different from ordinary stress?

Ordinary stress often has one clear source. The holiday rush is different because it is many small sources at once, and none of them feels large enough to justify stopping. A group chat needs a reply. A delivery window needs checking. A family plan needs a decision. Each item takes a minute, but together they fill every gap in the day, so there is never a moment when your attention is actually unclaimed.

That is why a long reading session rarely helps in this season. Opening a book or a long article becomes one more item on the list, and finishing it becomes one more thing to do well. A single verse asks for something else: read a few lines, stop, and notice whether you are present for the next thing you do, rather than already rehearsing the three things after it.

## How does Daily Dhamma work, step by step?

On our [Daily Dhamma product page](/dailydharma) we describe the app in three plain parts, and that is still exactly how it works today, 22 November 2026.

First, you swipe through curated verses from the Dhammapada in a focused reading view. You can choose light or dark mode for the way you like to read. There is no feed to catch up on and no backlog that grows when you miss a day.

Second, you can turn on a morning verse notification and Stay Present reminders during the day. The reminder asks a single question — "Are you present right now?" — as an invitation to stop and notice the moment. On the App Store listing the reminder choices are 5, 7, or 10 times a day.

Third, you save the verses that stay with you. Bookmarking is how a one-day reading becomes a small personal collection you can return to when the same kind of crowded day comes back.

The app is free to download. Premium includes access to all curated verses in the app, verse bookmarking, and up to 10 mindfulness reminders a day. Our product page says to review the current purchase offer in the app, and we repeat that here: we do not state a fixed Premium price in this article because the offer you see in the app is the one that applies to you.

## What verse do we return to when the rush turns into irritation?

The verse quoted on our own App Store listing is Verse 5: "Hatreds never cease through hatred in this world; through love alone they cease. This is an eternal law."

We return to it in this season for a practical reason. Crowded days shorten our patience, and the first place that shows is in how we reply to the people closest to us — a shorter message, a sharper tone, a decision made to end a conversation rather than to understand it. Reading Verse 5 does not remove the queue of tasks. It changes the state we bring to the next reply. That pause, repeated, is the whole practice this app is built around: one teaching at a time, in the middle of an ordinary day, not after the day becomes quiet.

If a verse stays with you, bookmark it. That is what the bookmark control on the reading screen is for, and over a few weeks those saved verses become a record of what actually helped, rather than a list of what you meant to read.

## How do we set reminders so they help instead of becoming more noise?

This is the question we hear most in busy weeks, and our answer is to start below the maximum. The listing offers 5, 7, or 10 reminders a day, and Premium includes up to 10. Starting at 10 because it is available turns a gentle prompt into another stream of notifications competing with everything else.

We suggest this order instead. Turn on the morning verse first, so the day starts with one verse before the messages start. Then choose the lowest Stay Present frequency, 5 times a day, for the first week. If you find yourself dismissing most of them without pausing, that is information: fewer, better-timed pauses are doing more work than many ignored ones. Raise the frequency only when the current one feels too sparse, not because a higher number looks more serious.

Dark mode matters here too, in a small way. Many people read the morning verse or the last verse of the day in bed or in a dim room. Choosing the mode you actually like to read in removes one tiny friction, and tiny frictions are what decide whether a daily practice survives a busy season.

## What do our measured App Store numbers say?

We only publish numbers we measured ourselves, with the period and source stated. The figures below come from App Store Connect analytics in our file apps-metrics-latest.json, measured at 2026-11-21T21:54:57Z.

For the 28 days from 24 October to 20 November 2026, Dhamma Quotes recorded 1,230 impressions, 41 product page views, and 16 downloads. Those downloads came from the United States (8), and one each from Nigeria, France, Ireland, Sri Lanka, Kazakhstan, the United Kingdom, Portugal, and Vietnam. By source, 9 came from App Store search, 4 from App Store browse, 2 from a web referrer, and 1 from an app referrer.

For the most recent 7 days in that file, 14 to 20 November 2026, the app recorded 479 impressions, 17 product page views, and 7 downloads — 3 from the United States and one each from Kazakhstan, the United Kingdom, Portugal, and Vietnam.

We read those numbers honestly. This is still a small app, and a week with 7 downloads is not a success story by itself. What it does show is that people in several countries are finding a one-verse-a-day app through search and browse in the weeks before the holidays, which is exactly the moment this guide is written for. We would rather show the real, small numbers with their dates than round them into a claim.

## What does Daily Dhamma not do?

It does not treat insomnia, anxiety, or any medical condition, and it is not a replacement for care. It does not require you to adopt a belief system to use it: the verses are presented as curated teachings from the Dhammapada that you can read, save, or pass by. And it does not try to hold your attention. There is no streak to protect and no feed to finish. If you read one verse and put the phone down, the app has done its job.

For the technical facts, checked on the App Store listing on 22 November 2026: the app is Dhamma Quotes: Buddha Quotes, version 1.2.1 (released 12 November), 44.3 MB, in the Health & Fitness category, in English, for iPhone, requiring iOS 15.1 or later. The listing states that data linked to you may include Purchases and Identifiers. You can read the full listing and decide for yourself here: [Dhamma Quotes on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/dhamma-quotes/id6757726663).

## How is this different from our last Daily Dhamma guide?

Our previous guide, [What can you do when your mind is racing at work or before sleep?](/blog/daily-dhamma-mind-racing-work-sleep-pause), was about a racing mind at a desk or in bed. This guide is about a different crowded state: the holiday rush, where the problem is not one looping thought but many small claims on your attention across the whole day. The practice is the same — one verse, a present-moment reminder, a saved verse to return to — but the setup is different: morning verse first, the lowest reminder frequency first, and Verse 5 as the verse we return to when patience runs short.

If affirmations are more your language than verses, our sister app [Anicca](/affirmation-app) works on the same principle in a different form: short daily cards rather than Dhammapada verses.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Daily Dhamma free?

Yes. Daily Dhamma is free to download, with in-app purchases. Premium includes all curated verses, verse bookmarking, and up to 10 mindfulness reminders a day. Review the current purchase offer in the app, because that is the offer that applies to you.

### How many reminders should I start with?

Start with the morning verse and 5 Stay Present reminders a day, the lowest frequency on the listing. Increase to 7 or 10 only if the current setting feels too sparse after a week of actually pausing at each reminder.

### Do I need to know anything about Buddhism to use it?

No. The app presents curated verses from the Dhammapada in a clean, distraction-free reading view. Whether you are new to Buddhism or a longtime practitioner, as our listing puts it, the use is the same: read one verse, notice the moment, and save the ones that stay with you.

### Which devices does it work on?

Daily Dhamma is listed for iPhone and requires iOS 15.1 or later. Check the App Store listing for current compatibility before you download.

### Where can I browse more Daily Dhamma guides?

On our [Daily Dhamma blog hub](/blog/c/daily-dhamma), where every guide for this app is collected, and on the [Daily Dhamma product page](/dailydharma).
